name: Kira Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Kira, 27, and I operate the drilling machine that makes holes for explosives at a large mine. I've got a two-year technical diploma and lead the drilling crew, although my wage is low for mining and I've barely three weeks of expenses put aside. I like getting a straight row of holes through awkward rock; I hate when a delayed repair steals the end of a shift. I use AI every day to help turn my rough maintenance notes into clear sentences, then check every number myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say better maintenance matters more than whether somebody's AI presentation impressed the managers at our mine. I still like my AI note helper, but I'd never let a neat sentence replace checking a drill fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drilling job looks steady in this picture, but my three-week reserve would vanish if I needed unpaid time off. I'm good at handling the drill; being good at work hasn't yet bought me a whole month without money worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the blast-hole drill and check every AI-assisted maintenance note against the fault sheet before sending it. I'd transfer fifteen each week into a repair fund after rent, rather than buy the new headphones I've been watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the ordinary stuff, especially being too ill to work a whole run of shifts. The AI picture itself barely changes my day, which doesn't make my bank balance any bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did that money worry last feel real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a tyre needed replacing and I kept comparing prices during lunch. I still did the job properly that afternoon, but all I could think about was whether the old tyre would last until payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you draw the line with the note helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I type the fault myself and ask for clearer wording without names or private records. If the tool changes a pressure reading, the original sheet wins and I correct the note before anyone uses it.

say: I'd say **better maintenance** matters more than whether somebody's AI presentation impressed the managers at our mine.
I still like my **AI note helper**, but I'd never let a neat sentence replace checking a drill fault.
think: The drilling job looks steady in this picture, but my **three-week reserve** would vanish if I needed unpaid time off.
I'm good at handling the drill; being **good at work** hasn't yet bought me a whole month without money worries.
do: Keep operating the **blast-hole drill** and check every AI-assisted maintenance note against the fault sheet before sending it.
Transfer **fifteen each week** into a repair fund after rent, rather than buy the new headphones I've been watching.
feel: **Anxious about a setback**, although the mine still seems to need her drilling skills.
S0.quote: I'm good at handling the drill; being good at work hasn't yet bought me a whole month without money worries.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** follows low reserves rather than expected displacement; daily tool use is narrow and checked against equipment records.
She separates **practical skill** from financial security, choosing a modest saving over a specific purchase rather than assuming spare income.

steps.text: Operate the drill and check assisted notes against original fault sheets
Save fifteen weekly in the repair fund instead of buying headphones

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for a drilling-plan trial if experienced operators can challenge the output before anyone changes the holes. The crew should share the time saved, rather than watch office jobs disappear while everybody else gets faster targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI can plan a pattern sooner than I can drill it, so my hands-on shifts still look secure for now. I'm interested in the software, but higher targets could make the same wage feel smaller if breaks keep getting squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join the planning-software trial and compare proposed drill rows with actual rock conditions during paid shifts. I'd bring breaks and targets to the crew meeting before the mine uses the trial to set new daily quotas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious enough to want a turn at the screen, and uneasy about what management counts as a benefit. I still expect to stay employed, but the three-week reserve leaves me anxious about any unpaid absence, just as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in a proposed pattern?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare hole spacing with the broken ground we actually saw on the last row. A plan that ignores where the drill struggled yesterday shouldn't get accepted just because the printout is tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise targets without blocking the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the recorded stoppages and ask for a joint review after a month. I want the trial to work safely, not to have every pause treated as proof the crew is lazy.

The crew should share the **time saved**, rather than watch office jobs disappear while everybody else gets faster targets.
think: AI can plan a pattern sooner than I can drill it, so my **hands-on shifts** still look secure for now.
I'm interested in the software, but **higher targets** could make the same wage feel smaller if breaks keep getting squeezed.
do: Ask to join the **planning-software trial** and compare proposed drill rows with actual rock conditions during paid shifts.
Bring **breaks and targets** to the crew meeting before the mine uses the trial to set new daily quotas.
feel: **Anxious about money**, with unease about quotas despite expecting her physical role to continue.
S1.quote: AI can plan a pattern sooner than I can drill it, so my hands-on shifts still look secure for now.
fieldNote: Her **early adoption** involves a supervised planning trial, with specific checks demonstrating practical experience rather than blind trust in software.
Her **collective request** targets working conditions; financial vulnerability continues despite expecting the physical drilling role to remain in the near term.

steps.text: Join the paid planning trial and compare drill patterns with rock conditions
Raise break protection and quota reviews at the crew meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew 2028 isn't the robot date, but waiting until robotic drills arrive around 2031 would waste our chance. The mine needs to fund paid learning, including for drivers who don't already enjoy trying new tools like I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect fewer drilling jobs once robots can do the hands-on work, and I can't fund a long wage gap. Learning fast helps me apply, but my thin savings mean I could still lose the flat while waiting for an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a paid control-room placement now and learn fault checking before thinking AI changes mine planning in 2028. I'd move the repair-fund balance into a rent reserve now and keep adding fifteen weekly through the first year after 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed because I can picture the mine buying a system and needing fewer of us, including me. Having ideas doesn't stop me waking up to count how many weeks the rent fund would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a control-room placement offer safety from thinking AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the screen work might change before my drilling does. I'd use the placement to understand faults and handovers while I'm still earning, then ask what roles actually remain instead of treating a new chair as protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029 if the placement was refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling while asking the worker representative for shared training time, with the refusal written down. I wouldn't pay for a long private course just because the mine's brochure said the future was exciting.

say: I'd tell the crew **2028** isn't the robot date, but waiting until robotic drills arrive around 2031 would waste our chance.
The mine needs to fund **paid learning**, including for drivers who don't already enjoy trying new tools like I do.
think: I expect **fewer drilling jobs** once robots can do the hands-on work, and I can't fund a long wage gap.
Learning fast helps me apply, but my **thin savings** mean I could still lose the flat while waiting for an answer.
do: Request a **paid control-room placement** now and learn fault checking before thinking AI changes mine planning in 2028.
Move the **repair-fund balance** into a rent reserve now and keep adding fifteen weekly through the first year after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed about lost pay**, despite a concrete willingness to learn new equipment early.
S2.quote: Learning fast helps me apply, but my thin savings mean I could still lose the flat while waiting for an answer.
fieldNote: She expects **earnings loss** from staffing cuts and later robotic drilling, with alarm supported by sleep disturbance and an inadequate household reserve.
The **placement request** offers learning despite its exposure; she recognises that moving from a drill to a screen cannot guarantee safety.

steps.text: Request a paid control-room placement focused on faults and handovers
Move the repair-fund balance into rent savings and add fifteen weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test training before the mine's thinking work changes in 2031. We need real placements, not a pile of certificates handed out when robotic drills arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with two years, I can build several months of rent if my wage stays steady and I stop upgrading devices. I'd still only be 32 in 2031, so the loss of a drilling career matters more than a single difficult year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current phone and send its planned replacement money to a rent reserve starting this payday. I'd take a short sensors course while working, then check actual equipment-support vacancies through the first year after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because I still expect a smaller drilling crew and don't know whether I'll be kept. The extra years let me try a course in small pieces and stop if it teaches nothing useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful sensors course teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to find out why an equipment sensor reports a fault and how someone checks whether the reading is true. I already understand the drilling machine from the cab, so I want a practical extension of that rather than a promise to become a completely different person overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes during 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling if the shifts remained and compare my course work with the faults the new planning system was actually reporting. The three years until robotic drills would be time to test a move, not a reason to forget the plan.

say: I'd say **five years** lets us test training before the mine's thinking work changes in 2031.
We need **real placements**, not a pile of certificates handed out when robotic drills arrive around 2034.
think: Compared with two years, I can build **several months of rent** if my wage stays steady and I stop upgrading devices.
I'd still only be **32 in 2031**, so the loss of a drilling career matters more than a single difficult year.
do: Keep my **current phone** and send its planned replacement money to a rent reserve starting this payday.
Take a **short sensors course** while working, then check actual equipment-support vacancies through the first year after 2031.
feel: **Anxious about a career**, with enough warning to test learning without immediately losing wages.
S3.quote: We need real placements, not a pile of certificates handed out when robotic drills arrive around 2034.
fieldNote: Her **career horizon** extends well beyond either automation date, so a longer warning improves her options without making the expected displacement harmless.
She makes **adaptability practical** through short study and vacancy checks alongside paid work, without assuming certificates create local demand.

steps.text: Keep the current phone and save the planned replacement money
Take a short sensors course and compare equipment-support vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade is enough to make learning ordinary rather than an emergency after a redundancy letter. By 2036 the planning may change completely; we should practise new equipment before robots reach drilling around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time to test several routes while earning, but few nearby employers still makes changing work difficult. My comfort with AI doesn't buy a guaranteed career, and I'd need proof of demand before borrowing money for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd arrange an equipment-supplier workshop this year and use paid leave only after confirming the session includes hands-on fault checks. I'd request an annual crew learning day, continuing the review through 2037 as planning work moves to thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm less frightened by the distant machine date, but I'm still anxious about how little money stands between me and missing rent now. Ten years gives me room to learn alongside work, not a reserve I can spend this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move away to use a new skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, but I haven't picked a place and I wouldn't pretend there are vacancies everywhere. I'd first ask workshop tutors where their former students actually found work, then compare the wages with moving costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual learning day achieve after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could check which tasks the new planning systems had really taken and which equipment still needed people. I'd want less confident crew members included, because a training day isn't useful if only the people who already like computers get a seat.

say: I'd tell the crew **a decade** is enough to make learning ordinary rather than an emergency after a redundancy letter.
By 2036 the planning may change completely; we should practise **new equipment** before robots reach drilling around 2039.
think: I'd have time to test several routes while earning, but **few nearby employers** still makes changing work difficult.
My comfort with AI doesn't buy a guaranteed career, and I'd need **proof of demand** before borrowing money for training.
do: Arrange an **equipment-supplier workshop** this year and use paid leave only after confirming the session includes hands-on fault checks.
Request an **annual crew learning day**, continuing the review through 2037 as planning work moves to thinking AI.
feel: **Anxious about present bills**, despite the longer warning allowing time to test several routes.
S4.quote: My comfort with AI doesn't buy a guaranteed career, and I'd need proof of demand before borrowing money for training.
fieldNote: She treats **ten years** as time for repeated low-cost experiments, while explicitly locating the major physical change around 2039 rather than 2036.
Concern for **shared access** persists, while limited reserves keep present anxiety alive despite the distant automation dates.

steps.text: Attend an equipment-supplier workshop with practical fault-checking exercises
Request annual crew learning days and review actual task changes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest picture because I expect the mine to need fewer people well before I've built a reserve. I'd want paid learning, a say for workers in equipment trials, and clear information on which actual jobs the training leads to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who has the energy to study after a long drilling shift. A paid hour learning a new machine is worth more to me than a free course after midnight.

headlineQuote: A paid hour learning a new machine is worth more to me than a free course after midnight.
portrait: A **27-year-old drill operator**, she leads a skilled crew, holds a technical diploma and enjoys solving problems with difficult rock.
Her **low mining wage** leaves only three weeks of expenses saved, even though she already uses AI daily to clarify maintenance notes.
She welcomes **worker-led trials** and wants paid learning shared across the crew, rather than benefits reserved for people with spare money.
Longer warning supports **tested study plans**, but she expects robotic drilling to threaten earnings and sees no skill as permanently protected.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut staffing before she has either a financial reserve or a route into another role.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid learning** and worker involvement in trials would make her willingness to experiment useful without sacrificing rent or sleep.
